title: What Would Happen if I Changed the Question https://ponderingplanning.wordpress.com/2026/09/09/what-would-happen-if-i-changed-the-question/
author: Paul Rowlandson
summary: A maths teacher makes the case for a single follow-up question after a worked example: what would happen if I changed the question. He distinguishes this from the usual retrospective use of variation theory, where students answer a set of minimally different items and then generalise, and positions it as forward-looking, asking students to predict the effect of a change before any calculation happens. He grounds the move in Douglas Newton's notion of forced prediction and in Anne Watson's account of dependency relations, then works through three purposes with concrete examples. First, separating superficially similar concepts: changing one value in a small dataset and asking which of mean, median, mode and range move, and why. Second, turning static questions into functional ones by treating the multiplicand or a numerator as a variable and asking how the product or quotient covaries. Third, extending problems so that a correct answer is stress-tested, most usefully in a cube-packing problem where raising the box height by two centimetres exposes that the divide-the-volumes method only works when the cubes fit exactly. The piece ends with a note that he keeps this to a little-and-often discussion after examples, and offers a slide bank for reuse.
points: The distinction he draws is between retrospective variation, reflecting on answers already found, and prospective prediction about questions not yet answered.
He anchors the technique in Newton's forced prediction, which obliges a learner to construct a mental model and reason step-wise from initial to final state.
The averages example asks which summary statistics change when a single data value moves, which forces attention onto the defining property of each one.
Asking why doubling the multiplicand and doubling the multiplier give different and identical products respectively surfaces covariation inside an otherwise fixed question.
The cube-packing example is the strongest move in the piece: a height change creates cognitive conflict and reveals a method that had been right by coincidence.
quotes: After completing a worked example on the board, one of my favourite questions to ask is, “What would happen if I changed the question?” More specifically, point to a number or term within the question, describe a change we could make to it and then ask how that would affect our original answer.

This could be viewed as a retrospective approach, where students reflect on answers they have found moments earlier. By contrast, asking “What would happen if I changed the question?” could be viewed as a forward-looking approach, prompting students to consider questions they have not yet answered.

He claims that “forced prediction obliges a learner to construct a mental model or otherwise make connections amongst pieces of information… Learners [are] required to predict step-wise from the initial state to the final state” (p.42).

It is not unusual for students to get mixed up between mean, median, mode and range. Mathematics is filled with concepts that can appear superficially similar, which students can be prone to mixing up.
Many questions students see in Key Stages 1-4 are somewhat ‘static’ in their nature. By that I mean all the parts of the question are fixed and therefore the answer is fixed.
I also find that students have a habit of thinking “job done” as soon as they solve a problem and then promptly cast it out of their mind as they move on to the next problem.

However, careful attention to the context would lead students to conclude that the answer should remain the same. As the cubes are 5 cm tall, you couldn’t physically fit any additional cubes into the extra 2 cm tall space at top of the box.
Dividing the volume of the box by the volume of the cube only gives the correct answer when the cubes fit exactly into the box, without leftover space.
